title: 10 Science Facts That Sound Made Up (But Are 100% True)
intro: Ten science facts that sound like somebody made them up. Every one is real and checked against NASA, a government agency or a published paper, with the sources in the description. We start with lightning hotter than the Sun, and we finish with the one that changes how you look at a glass of water. Let's go.

segments.heading: Lightning is five times hotter than the Sun's surface
segments.text: A bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The United States National Weather Service puts the number at around fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit, roughly twenty-seven thousand degrees Celsius. The Sun's visible surface, by comparison, is a relatively cool fifty-five hundred degrees Celsius. The heat is over in a flash, which is why a tree gets scorched rather than turned to ash. But the air in the path of the bolt gets so hot, so fast, that it expands violently, then cools and snaps back together. That sudden expansion and contraction makes a sound wave, and that sound wave is thunder. So every rumble in a storm is the sound of air being heated hotter than a star. Count the seconds between the flash and the bang, and you are timing the echo of something hotter than the Sun.

segments.heading: Honey never goes off
segments.text: Honey never goes off. Archaeologists opening ancient Egyptian tombs have found pots of honey that are thousands of years old and still perfectly edible. Three things keep it that way. First, honey is almost all sugar and has very little water, so bacteria and moulds simply dry out and die inside it. Second, it is acidic, with a pH between about three and four and a half, which most microbes can't stand. Third, bees add an enzyme called glucose oxidase that slowly produces hydrogen peroxide, the same stuff you clean a cut with. Amina Harris, who runs the Honey and Pollination Center at the University of California, Davis, explains that as long as the jar stays sealed and no water gets in, it will last indefinitely. The jar at the back of your cupboard is basically immortal. It just might have gone crunchy.

segments.heading: Bananas are radioactive
segments.text: Bananas are radioactive. Not dangerously, but measurably. Bananas are rich in potassium, and a small fraction of all potassium on Earth is potassium-40, which is naturally radioactive. A single banana gives off so many little flashes of radiation that a lorry full of them can set off the radiation detectors that are looking for smuggled nuclear material. Physicists even joke about the banana equivalent dose. But here is the twist. You are more radioactive than a banana. An average adult carries about 140 grams of potassium, including around sixteen milligrams of the radioactive kind, which makes you roughly 280 times more radioactive than the fruit. Eat a banana and your potassium-40 goes up by less than half a percent, and your body flushes the extra out within a few hours. You can't become radioactive by eating bananas. You already are.

segments.heading: The centre of the Earth is as hot as the Sun's surface
segments.text: The centre of the Earth is as hot as the surface of the Sun. In 2013, a French team led by Agnès Dewaele squeezed tiny specks of iron between two diamonds to pressures of more than two million atmospheres, heated them with lasers, and fired an X-ray beam from the European Synchrotron in Grenoble through them to see the exact moment the iron melted. From that, they worked out the temperature where the solid inner core meets the liquid outer core: about six thousand degrees Celsius, give or take five hundred. That is a thousand degrees hotter than the previous estimate, and it matches the Sun's visible surface, which NASA puts at fifty-five hundred degrees. The pressure down there is so enormous that the iron stays solid anyway. You are standing on a crust a few dozen kilometres thick, floating over a ball of metal as hot as a star.

segments.heading: Everest is not the closest point to space
segments.text: The top of Mount Everest is not the point on Earth closest to space. That title goes to a volcano in Ecuador called Chimborazo, which is more than two and a half kilometres lower than Everest. The reason is that the Earth is not a perfect ball. It spins, and that spin pushes the middle outward, so the planet is fatter around the equator. Everest sits far to the north, on the thinner part. Chimborazo sits almost on the equator, on top of the bulge. Measure from the centre of the Earth instead of from sea level, and the summit of Chimborazo is about two thousand and seventy metres farther out than Everest, according to the US ocean agency NOAA. So if you want to stand as far from the centre of the planet as possible, go to Ecuador. Everest climbers will not want to hear this.

segments.heading: The Eiffel Tower leans away from the Sun
segments.text: The Eiffel Tower leans away from the Sun. On a clear day, the top of the tower slowly moves in a circle about fifteen centimetres across, following the Sun around the sky but always tilting away from it. The tower is built from iron, and iron expands when it gets warm. The side facing the Sun heats up and stretches, while the shaded side stays cool and short, so the whole structure bends gently away from the heat. The tower's own operators describe it on their official site: the structure gains or loses a few centimetres over the year, grows a little in summer, and shrinks again in winter. Gustave Eiffel's engineers had spent twenty years building iron viaducts, so they knew exactly how the metal behaves. The most famous landmark in Paris is quietly dancing in a circle every sunny day, and nobody looking up can tell.

segments.heading: A teaspoon of soil holds a billion bacteria
segments.text: A single teaspoon of healthy soil can hold up to a billion bacteria. Ohio State University's extension service gives the range at one hundred million to one billion in a teaspoon of productive soil, and that is just the bacteria. Add the fungi, the protozoa, the tiny worms and the mites, and soil scientists say there are more living things in a teaspoon of soil than there are people on Earth. Those organisms are the reason anything grows. They break dead plants down into food for new ones, help the ground hold water, and the fungi grow long threads that wrap around roots and feed them. A patch of ground that looks like dirt is one of the most crowded places on the planet. The next time you wipe your boots, you have just evicted a city.

segments.heading: Every second breath you take comes from the ocean
segments.text: At least half of all the oxygen on Earth is made in the ocean. Not by the rainforests, by the sea. The US ocean agency NOAA says most of it comes from plankton, tiny drifting plants and bacteria that float near the surface and do what trees do: take in sunlight and carbon dioxide and breathe out oxygen. One of them, a bacterium called Prochlorococcus, is the smallest photosynthetic organism known, and one of the most abundant cells in the sea. That one species alone produces up to a fifth of the oxygen in the biosphere, more than every tropical rainforest on land put together. And nobody even knew it existed until 1986, when a team from Woods Hole and Harvard spotted it. So take a breath. Roughly every second one came from something you need a microscope to see, floating somewhere in the sea.

segments.heading: Sunlight is 170,000 years old when it leaves the Sun
segments.text: The sunlight hitting your face took about eight minutes to cross space from the Sun. But the energy in it was made around one hundred and seventy thousand years ago. In the core of the Sun, hydrogen atoms fuse together and release energy as light. The problem is that the inside of the Sun is so dense that each bit of light can only travel a tiny distance before it bumps into something and bounces off in a random direction. So it staggers outward, step by step, like a drunk trying to leave a crowded room. NASA puts the trip from the core to the top of the convection zone at about one hundred and seventy thousand years. Only then does it escape into space and reach us in minutes. The light warming you now was born before modern humans left Africa.

segments.heading: Some of the water in your glass is older than the Sun
segments.text: And the one that changes how you look at a glass of water. A big share of the water on Earth is older than the Sun. In 2014, Ilsedore Cleeves and her team at the University of Michigan rebuilt the early solar system in a computer, the giant disc of gas and dust the planets formed from. They looked at heavy water, which has an extra neutron in its hydrogen. Today's oceans, comets and meteorites hold more heavy water than the young solar system could have made on its own. The only explanation is that much of our water formed earlier, as ice in the freezing cloud between the stars, and survived the birth of the Sun. Their paper in Science estimates that between thirty and fifty percent of Earth's ocean water is older than the Sun, which is about four point six billion years old. Every sip, part interstellar.

outro: So that's lightning hotter than the Sun, honey that never spoils, and water older than the solar system. Which fact are you going to tell someone tomorrow? Put it in the comments. There's a new fact here every evening.
description:
Ten science facts that sound made up but are completely true, from lightning five times hotter than the Sun and a volcano that beats Everest to the water in your glass that is older than the Sun. Every one is checked against NASA, a government agency or a published paper; the sources are listed below.
Which one are you telling someone tomorrow?
